common_name: Lady Betty Balfour Clematis (Vigorous Late-Season Violet-Purple Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Lady Betty Balfour flowers only on the current season's growth, so cut the whole vine back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3).

directions: A vigorous old English cultivar notable for flowering later than most large-flowered hybrids, Lady Betty Balfour bears rich violet-purple flowers with contrasting cream-yellow stamens from late summer into early fall. Because it blooms entirely on new wood, the whole vine can be pruned hard every late winter, and its late display extends the clematis season after many spring- and early-summer-flowering types have finished. Its climbing habit and dependable late color have kept it a long-standing choice for covering a pergola or large fence.

common_name: Madame Baron Veillard Clematis (Pale Lilac-Pink Latest-Blooming Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Mme Baron Veillard flowers on both old and new wood, so light pruning (Group 2) preserves the early flush while still allowing its characteristically late repeat bloom.

directions: Raised in France in the 1880s, Mme Baron Veillard bears rounded, pale lilac-pink flowers with a faint mauve cast, among the latest large-flowered clematis to open each year, often continuing into early fall after most other hybrids have finished. Its exceptional vigor and tolerance of a wide range of soils have kept it in cultivation for well over a century, and its soft, unassuming color pairs easily with stronger-colored companions nearby. Light pruning in late winter preserves the earliest buds while still encouraging its long late-season display.

common_name: Westerplatte Clematis (Velvety Deep Red Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Westerplatte flowers on both old and new wood, so light pruning (Group 2) preserves the early flush while still encouraging a strong repeat bloom.

directions: Bred in Poland by the noted clematis hybridizer Brother Stefan Franczak and named for the site of the opening battle of World War II in Gdansk, Westerplatte bears velvety, deep red flowers with a slightly darker bar and golden stamens. It flowers from early summer on the previous year's growth, with a repeat flush on new growth into late summer, so pruning should stay light and be timed just after the first bloom. Its intensely saturated color has made it one of the more widely grown of Franczak's many Polish-bred clematis introductions.

common_name: Arctic Queen Clematis (Double Creamy White Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Arctic Queen flowers double on old wood in early summer, so prune only lightly right after the main flush (Group 2) to keep the doubled blooms.

directions: A modern large-flowered hybrid from the Raymond Evison breeding program, Arctic Queen opens fully double, creamy white flowers with a hint of pale green at the base of each tepal on the previous year's growth in early summer. A later flush produced on new growth later in the season is typically single rather than double, giving the vine two distinct looks across the year. Its crisp white double blooms and compact habit have made it a popular choice for a container or a modest trellis near a patio.

common_name: Kiri Te Kanawa Clematis (Double Rich Blue Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Kiri Te Kanawa flowers double on old wood in early summer, so prune only lightly right after the main flush (Group 2) to preserve the doubled blooms.

directions: Bred by Raymond Evison and named for the celebrated New Zealand opera soprano, Kiri Te Kanawa produces fully double, rich violet-blue flowers with a rosette of narrower inner tepals layered over the broader outer ones, opening on the previous year's growth in late spring to early summer. A lighter single-flowered repeat bloom can follow on new growth later in the season. Its saturated blue color and elegant double form have made it a sought-after modern large-flowered cultivar for a prominent obelisk or pillar.

common_name: Carnaby Clematis (Raspberry-Pink Large-Flowered Clematis with Deep Pink Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Carnaby flowers on both old and new wood, so light pruning (Group 2) preserves the early flush while still allowing a strong repeat bloom.

directions: Bred by Raymond Evison, Carnaby bears raspberry-pink flowers with a bold, deep pink central bar down each tepal, opening on the previous year's growth from late spring and repeating on new growth through summer into fall. Its vivid, long-lasting color and naturally compact, well-branched habit compared to older large-flowered hybrids have made it one of the more widely sold modern clematis for a container or a modest trellis near a doorway.

common_name: Avant Garde Clematis (Unusual Semi-Double Magenta Clematis with Green-White Center)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Avant Garde flowers on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3).

directions: A distinctive modern hybrid from the Evison-Poulsen breeding program, Avant Garde produces unusual semi-double, magenta-pink outer tepals surrounding a dense central cluster of shorter greenish-white petaloid stamens, giving each flower an anemone-like, two-tiered look unlike typical large-flowered clematis. Blooming from midsummer into fall on new growth, the whole vine can be cut back hard each late winter, and its unconventional flower form has made it a conversation piece among gardeners who already grow the more classic large-flowered types.

common_name: Picardy Clematis (Compact Mauve-Pink Patio Clematis with Deeper Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Picardy flowers on both old and new wood, so light pruning (Group 2) preserves the earliest flush while still allowing a strong repeat bloom.

directions: Part of the Raymond Evison Boulevard Collection bred for naturally compact growth, Picardy bears mauve-pink flowers with a deeper rosy-mauve central bar on a restrained vine well suited to a patio container. It flowers over an extended season from early summer into fall on both old and new growth, so light pruning preserves the earliest blooms while still allowing strong repeat flowering. Its manageable size and long display make it an easy option for gardeners without room for a full-sized clematis.

common_name: Mrs Spencer Castle Clematis (Double Mauve-Pink Early-Season Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; prune lightly (Group 2) to preserve the double flowers that form on old wood, since flowers produced later on new growth will be single.

directions: An English cultivar dating to the early twentieth century, Mrs Spencer Castle opens fully double, soft mauve-pink flowers in late spring on the previous year's growth, with a later flush on new growth typically single rather than double. Its old-fashioned double form, reminiscent of a small peony, has kept it in circulation among collectors even as many of its Victorian- and Edwardian-era contemporaries have faded from commerce, and it rewards the light, careful pruning needed to protect the wood that produces its doubled blooms.

common_name: Victoria Clematis (Rosy-Mauve Large-Flowered Clematis with Reflexed Tepals)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Victoria flowers on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3).

directions: An English cultivar dating to the 1870s, Victoria bears rosy-mauve flowers with a slightly darker bar and gently reflexed, twisting tepals that give each bloom a loose, informal shape compared to the flatter form of many large-flowered hybrids. It flowers abundantly on the current season's growth from midsummer into early fall, so the whole vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter. Its long bloom period and tolerance of hard annual pruning have kept it a dependable choice for well over a century.

common_name: John Treasure Clematis (Deep Blue-Purple Viticella-Type Clematis with Cream Stamens)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; John Treasure is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: Raised at the Washfield Nursery in England and named for its noted plantsman proprietor, John Treasure bears richly colored, deep blue-purple flowers with contrasting cream-yellow stamens that stand out sharply against the dark tepals. Like other viticella-type cultivars it flowers prolifically from midsummer into early fall on the current season's growth, so the entire vine can be cut back hard each late winter. Its saturated color and easy, hard-pruned care have made it a favorite for scrambling through a spent early-summer shrub or climbing rose.

common_name: Allanah Clematis (Deep Red Large-Flowered Clematis with Golden Stamens)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Allanah flowers on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3).

directions: Raised by the English Jackman nursery, Allanah bears richly saturated, velvety red flowers with contrasting golden-yellow stamens on broad, overlapping tepals. It flowers abundantly on the current season's growth from midsummer into early fall, so the whole vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter. Its deep, clear red color and tolerance of hard annual pruning have made it a dependable choice for a sunny fence or trellis where a strong red accent is wanted among cooler blue and purple clematis.

common_name: Mega Mindy Hydrangea (Sturdy Pink-to-Red Aging Panicle Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Mega Mindy blooms on new wood, so prune hard in late winter to stimulate strong new growth and maximum flowering.

directions: A Belgian-bred panicle hydrangea selected for strong, sturdy stems that hold its dense flower panicles upright without flopping even after rain, Mega Mindy opens creamy white in summer and gradually deepens through pink to a dusky red-pink as the flowers age into fall. Its compact, well-branched habit and reliable color change have made it a popular landscape selection alongside better-known introductions like Pinky Winky and Vanille Fraise. Like other H. paniculata cultivars it blooms on new wood, so prune hard in late winter to a low framework of buds for the strongest flowering and sturdiest stems.
